Classification guard: the authored edge asserts association only (etiologicalConsensus NOT_ESTABLISHED, vaNexusProbabilityAlignment NOT_ASSERTED, hypothesizedOnly:true, mechanismCategory IMMUNE_MEDIATED). The located cohort is small, contemporaneous, and same-source (34 patients infected simultaneously), and urticaria and angioedema are partly constitutive of the acute syndrome rather than a distinct downstream disorder, so the edge records case-matching of the presentation; individual claims require parasitological or serological confirmation of the acute infection, dermatologic documentation of the urticaria with chronology, and exclusion of the competing causes listed on the edge.

Stage and direction guards: no katayama-fever-to-pulmonary-hypertension edge is authored - the located schistosomiasis-associated pulmonary arterial hypertension literature concerns chronic, largely hepatosplenic disease with portal hypertension rather than the acute Katayama phase, so the proposition would cross disease stages; no anemia or malnutrition-residuals edge is authored for the same reason (chronic-phase outcomes authored by their own primaries).

Wrong-target and duplicate-scope guards: no katayama-fever-to-tropical-pulmonary-eosinophilia or eosinophilic-gastroenteritis edge is authored - those are distinct disease entities with their own aetiologies (filarial and gastrointestinal respectively) rather than consequences of acute schistosomiasis; the urticaria identity currently receives one window (thyroiditis), so this window is not pre-empted, and no hepatitis, angioedema, or respiratory edge is authored because angioedema has no catalog identity, acute-phase schistosomal hepatitis was not located at condition-specific level, and the pulmonary findings are constitutive of the syndrome.
governanceNotes: D1 batch 50 (2026-09-24): one bounded association edge authored - Katayama fever to urticaria (rank 1) - classified ASSOCIATION_ONLY with etiologicalConsensus NOT_ESTABLISHED, vaNexusProbabilityAlignment NOT_ASSERTED, and hypothesizedOnly:true; mechanismCategory IMMUNE_MEDIATED. The proposition rests on the Rocha 1995 study of the secondary cutaneous manifestations of acute schistosomiasis mansoni, which followed 34 patients infected simultaneously at the same location and found that 16 developed angioedema and/or urticaria, generally of short duration and mild intensity and usually appearing about 30 days after infection, with no apparent association between the skin manifestations and worm burden, blood eosinophilia, or areas of immediate reaction to intradermal worm antigen so that the authors attributed them to host immunological reactivity; it rests also on the Wilder-Smith and Caumes 2024 clinical review of skin problems in travellers, which states that acute schistosomiasis is the most common parasitic cause of acute urticaria in travellers within a pruritus-associated differential that also includes cercarial dermatitis, scabies, and creeping dermatitis. Cutaneous immunoallergic manifestations are thus documented as part of the acute schistosomal syndrome.

Counter-evidence and caveat screens recorded 2026-09-24: (i) constitutive overlap - urticaria and angioedema are features of the acute syndrome itself rather than a separate disease arising from it, so the edge is framed as case-matching of the presentation at association-only strength, mirroring the glomus-tumor-to-chronic-pain precedent; (ii) mechanism-independence of the finding - the located cohort found the skin manifestations independent of worm burden and eosinophilia, which the authors read as host-immunoreactivity-driven, so the edge does not rest on parasite-load reasoning; (iii) small contemporaneous cohort - 34 simultaneously infected patients from a single outbreak with 16 affected, so no population-level incidence can be inferred and the interval of about 30 days is cohort-specific; (iv) broad differential - acute urticaria in travellers and in endemic populations has many causes, and the review's own differential lists cercarial dermatitis, scabies, and creeping dermatitis, so competing causes must be excluded clinically.

Negative screens recorded 2026-09-24: (i) no pulmonary-hypertension edge - the schistosomiasis-associated pulmonary arterial hypertension literature concerns chronic hepatosplenic disease with portal hypertension rather than the acute phase (stage guard); (ii) no anemia or malnutrition-residuals edge - those outcomes belong to chronic schistosomiasis and are authored from their own primaries (stage and duplicate-scope guards); (iii) no tropical-pulmonary-eosinophilia or eosinophilic-gastroenteritis edge - those are distinct disease identities with their own aetiologies (wrong-target guard); (iv) no angioedema edge - there is no angioedema identity in the catalogue (absent-identity guard); (v) no hepatitis edge - no condition-specific acute-phase schistosomal hepatitis quantification was located in this batch window (zero-record guard); (vi) no pulmonary-fibrosis or pneumothorax edge - no acute or chronic schistosomal quantification for those outcomes was located (zero-record guard); (vii) duplicate-scope note: the urticaria identity receives one window (thyroiditis), so this window is not pre-empted.

nexusClaim.associationBasis: The Rocha 1995 study of secondary cutaneous manifestations of acute schistosomiasis mansoni followed 34 patients infected simultaneously at the same location and found that 16 developed angioedema and/or urticaria, generally of short duration and mild intensity and usually appearing about 30 days after infection, with no apparent association between the skin manifestations and worm burden, blood eosinophilia, or immediate intradermal reaction to worm antigen, leading the authors to attribute the manifestations to host immunological reactivity; the Wilder-Smith and Caumes 2024 clinical review of skin problems in travellers states that acute schistosomiasis is the most common parasitic cause of acute urticaria in travellers, within a pruritus-associated differential that also includes cercarial dermatitis, scabies, and creeping dermatitis; the literature documents urticaria and angioedema as manifestations of the acute schistosomal syndrome without establishing that the syndrome caused an individual's urticarial episode.
nexusClaim.causationStatus: The mapping does not assert that the acute schistosomal syndrome caused an individual's urticaria: urticaria and angioedema are partly constitutive of the acute syndrome itself rather than a distinct downstream disorder, so the edge records case-matching of the presentation; the located cohort was small and contemporaneous and found the manifestations independent of worm burden and eosinophilia, and acute urticaria has many alternative causes in the same populations (viral infection, drug or food exposure, cercarial dermatitis, scabies, and other parasitic infection) - so no directional claim is made.

causalMechanism.primaryVector: A hypothesized host-immunoreactivity route is described: as schistosomula migrate and maturing worms begin egg deposition roughly two to six weeks after cercarial penetration, a systemic immunoallergic reaction develops - the febrile, eosinophilic acute syndrome known as Katayama fever - and in a proportion of patients it presents cutaneously as acute urticaria and angioedema; the located cohort found the skin manifestations independent of worm burden and eosinophilia, which the authors read as evidence that host immunological reactivity rather than parasite load generates them. Because the cutaneous eruption overlaps the syndrome definition itself and has many competing causes, the individual pathway remains a hypothesis.

evidentiaryProfile.conservativeRationale: This relationship is supported as an association only. Urticaria and angioedema are documented in a substantial proportion of a defined same-source cohort with acute schistosomiasis and are recognised as the commonest parasitic cause of acute urticaria in travellers, but individual determination requires parasitological or serological confirmation of the acute infection, dermatologic documentation of the urticaria with chronology, exclusion of other causes of acute urticaria, and review by a qualified medical professional.
evidentiaryProfile.evidenceGaps: Parasitological or serological confirmation of acute schistosomiasis with species where available (seroconversion, stool or urine ova, or species-specific serology) together with the date of freshwater exposure and the interval from exposure to presentation; travel and exposure history with location, dates, and water contact; documentation of the urticaria or angioedema (distribution, duration, recurrence, angioedema involvement, and dermatographism) with dates relative to both exposure and treatment; the accompanying syndrome features (fever, cough, myalgia, headache, abdominal tenderness, eosinophil count, and any imaging findings); testing excluding other causes of acute urticaria (infection, drug and food triggers, thyroid autoimmunity, other parasitic infection, and chronic spontaneous urticaria) and exclusion of cercarial dermatitis or scabies as the observed eruption; qualified clinical assessment of whether the acute schistosomal infection materially contributed to the urticarial episode
alternativeEtiologiesToRuleOut: Acute urticaria from another cause (viral or bacterial infection, drug exposure, food, or contactant)
Cercarial dermatitis (swimmer's itch) rather than urticaria as the observed eruption
Scabies, cutaneous larva migrans, or another travel-associated dermatosis
Chronic spontaneous or autoimmune urticaria (for example autoimmune-thyroiditis-associated)
Angioedema from ACE-inhibitor or other pharmacological exposure
Another parasitic infection presenting with urticaria and eosinophilia (strongyloidiasis, ascariasis, toxocariasis)

evidenceGaps: Parasitological or serological confirmation of acute schistosomiasis with species where available (seroconversion, stool or urine ova, or species-specific serology) together with the date of freshwater exposure and the interval from exposure to presentation; travel and exposure history with location, dates, and water contact; documentation of the urticaria or angioedema (distribution, duration, recurrence, angioedema involvement, and dermatographism) with dates relative to both exposure and treatment; the accompanying syndrome features (fever, cough, myalgia, headache, abdominal tenderness, eosinophil count, and any imaging findings); testing excluding other causes of acute urticaria (infection, drug and food triggers, thyroid autoimmunity, other parasitic infection, and chronic spontaneous urticaria) and exclusion of cercarial dermatitis or scabies as the observed eruption; qualified clinical assessment of whether the acute schistosomal infection materially contributed to the urticarial episode
suggestions.rationale: Authored at ASSOCIATION_ONLY: a same-source cohort of 34 simultaneously infected patients with acute schistosomiasis mansoni found urticaria and/or angioedema in 16 patients at about 30 days post-infection and independent of worm burden and eosinophilia, and a travel-medicine review identifies acute schistosomiasis as the most common parasitic cause of acute urticaria. Because the cutaneous eruption is partly constitutive of the acute syndrome and the cohort is small and contemporaneous, the conservative standard keeps the edge at association only; the urticaria identity receives one window at present (thyroiditis), so this window is not pre-empted.
